c.v: Two problems, neither one met before, 45 minutes between them and a hard stop on each. Read a problem once, write down the pattern and the complexity you expect, then code it with a
that tests the cases the statement names, closed book. Move on when the time for a problem is up whether or not it runs, and note where you stopped before you look at what a good answer contains.
The first problem: a relay network is wired as a rooted binary tree,
struct Node { int id = 0; std::unique_ptr<Node> left; std::unique_ptr<Node> right; };
, each relay linking to at most two child relays below it, at most 20,000 relays in total. Write

, which returns the greatest number of relays on any path between two relays in the network. The path may go up through a relay the two share and back down the other side, so it does not have to pass through the root, and it counts every relay on it once, endpoints included. An empty network returns 0, and a single relay returns 1. Take a
. Give yourself 22 minutes, and state the time and extra space in terms of the relay count n and the tree's height h.

A strong answer at 22 minutes has the recursion returning the height of the subtree it was called on while folding the best chain seen anywhere below it into a running value passed by reference or returned alongside the height, tests the four shapes named below, and states O(n) time with O(h) stack space. A partial answer gets the height right but only checks chains through the root, missing a longer one lower down, such as the case where the longest chain passes through an internal relay but never reaches the root at all. A weak answer recomputes the height of every subtree from scratch at every node, which still finds the right answer but costs O(n²) on a chain, or cannot say why the extra space is the height rather than the relay count.

Test an empty network, a single relay, a straight chain of four relays where the longest chain is the whole thing, a tree where the longest chain passes through an internal relay but not through the root, and a balanced tree of seven relays where the longest chain runs from one bottom corner to the other through the root.
The second problem: a rover's planner holds a list of hops between numbered waypoints, each hop tagged with a roughness rating,
struct Hop { std::ptrdiff_t a; std::ptrdiff_t b; std::int64_t roughness; };
, crossable in either direction. At most 500 waypoints, numbered 0 to n − 1, at most 2000 hops, and roughness a positive integer up to 1,000,000. Write
, which returns the smallest value R such that a route from
exists using only hops with roughness at most R, or no value when no route connects them even using every hop available.
returns 0 without looking at the hops at all. Take
. Give yourself 23 minutes, and state the time in terms of the waypoint count n and the hop count m.

A strong answer at 23 minutes notices that a route surviving at roughness R also survives at any roughness above R, which is what makes the answer searchable: sort the distinct roughness values, and binary search for the smallest one where a reachability check, breadth-first or depth-first over only the hops at or under it, connects

. That is O((n + m) log m) time, one check of O(n + m) for each of O(log m) candidates. A partial answer gets a correct but linear scan over the sorted roughness values instead of a binary search, which is O(m (n + m)) and still passes every test at this size; binary searches correctly but rebuilds the sorted list of roughness values with duplicates left in, which wastes checks without changing the answer; or binary searches by arithmetic midpoint over the raw range of possible roughness values, 0 to 1,000,000, checking reachability at each midpoint tried rather than at a value some hop actually has. That last one still terminates and still finds the right answer, because the reachability predicate is monotone in R whichever values are tried, only at O((n + m) log R) for the value range R instead of O((n + m) log m) for the roughness values that occur, dearer whenever m is far smaller than R. A weak answer's binary search moves its lower bound with
comes back true, which never advances once
from 0 to 3, where the cheapest route that avoids the 9 goes 0 to 2 to 3 at a worst hop of 7; the same graph from

to itself; the same graph from 1 to 3; a fifth waypoint with no hop touching it, which must return no value; a single direct hop; and a chain of three hops that all share the same roughness, where the answer is that roughness as soon as any path exists at all.

Take 15 minutes. For each problem you did not finish cleanly, in the strong-answer sense above, write three lines: which of the two problems, the exact place your approach diverged from the strong answer (the wrong quantity carried up the recursion, a linear scan instead of a binary search, a hand-rolled midpoint instead of a search over the candidates that occur), and the one exercise you will redo closed book before the next timed mock. For the relay chain, that exercise is
, which also carries a value up from every node in the tree rather than only down; for the roughness problem, it is
's exercise on searching a rotated array, which is the same lesson in binary searching on a computed condition rather than on the array's raw values.

Count a problem solved only when it passes every test named in its statement inside its time limit. Two solved is a pass. One solved, with a written cause and a named exercise for the other, is a fair stopping point for today and a re-attempt in a week, closed book, before the follow-up exercise. Neither solved inside its time is a sign the two prerequisite topics need another pass before a fifth mock is worth attempting.
